text:
Accurate Designation and Retained Human Moral Authority in Federal Use of Computational Systems

Saturday, October 3, 2026
Dr. Joel Rutkowski
Policy Memorandum

Note to reader: All verses quoted are from "King James Version."

Executive Summary

Federal agencies should describe large language models and related systems according to their actual operations—storage and statistical processing of data—and should retain final moral and legal authority exclusively with human officials. The executive-branch preference for the label “Super Intelligence” is a euphemism. It misdescribes present systems, conflicts with the prior technical meaning of that term, and risks acclimating the public to premises that lack support in the philosophical, technical, and theological record from 1950 to 2026.

Human beings alone bear the moral status recognized in the American legal inheritance and, for many citizens, in the biblical account of creation in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27). Machines store and process data. They do not understand, originate moral judgments, or bear responsibility. Martin Heidegger’s analysis of technology as enframing supplies an independent philosophical warning: calculative ordering is not the same as thoughtful decision. Policy should enforce accurate nomenclature, non-delegation of final decisions, and interface honesty without restricting research or technological competition.

I. Purpose

This memorandum recommends executive and, where necessary, legislative measures so that official language and administrative procedure remain consistent with the observable properties of computational systems and with the unique moral agency of human persons.

II. Background

Aubrey Harris, writing in The American Spectator on 30 September 2026 (https://t.co/fhn5DgUNAo), argues that names shape thought. Drawing on G. K. Chesterton and George Orwell, the article treats the redesignation of artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence” as euphemism that obscures mechanism. Three claims are central. First, “super intelligence” already denotes, in the technical literature, systems capable of outperforming humans across cognitive domains—a threshold present frontier models have not met. Second, large language models generate text by next-token prediction over neural networks trained on large corpora; they have not demonstrated independent comprehension or novel concept formation of the kind ordinary in human children. Third, humans remain human and machines remain machines; neither apocalyptic prohibition nor uncritical merger is warranted.

White House language accompanying the order asserts that frontier systems “do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence” and therefore justify the new designation. That assertion is a branding choice, not a result established in cognitive science.

III. Biblical Frame

Genesis 1:26–27 states: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” Genesis 9:6 links that status to the protection of human life. Historic interpretation locates the image in rational and moral agency, relational capacity, and accountable dominion, not in information throughput. Psalm 8 and Colossians 3:10 likewise treat the image as proper to human persons. Nothing in the text extends created moral status to artifacts. Machines may serve as instruments; moral standing and final judgment remain human.

IV. Literature Review, 1950–2026

Computation and behavioral tests (1950–1980). Alan Turing’s 1950 imitation game defined success behaviorally and set aside inner understanding. Claude Shannon’s information theory and John von Neumann’s architecture supplied the engineering foundation. Early functionalism proposed that mental states might be realized in non-biological substrates. John Searle’s 1980 Chinese Room argument replied that syntactic manipulation of symbols, however fluent, does not constitute semantic understanding or intentionality.

Heidegger and the essence of technology. Martin Heidegger’s 1954 essay “The Question Concerning Technology” appeared in the same early period and remains the most influential philosophical account of modern technics. Heidegger argued that the essence of technology is not the machines themselves but Gestell, or enframing: a mode of revealing in which everything, including the human being, is ordered as standing-reserve (Bestand), on call for further ordering. Calculative thinking, which computes and optimizes, is distinguished from meditative thinking, which waits upon what shows itself. Enframing does not merely use tools; it constricts the range of what can appear as worthy of decision. Applied to contemporary systems, the analysis is direct. A model that stores data and predicts tokens operates wholly inside calculative ordering. It cannot step outside the frame to ask whether the optimization itself ought to be pursued. Heidegger did not live to see large language models, yet the reduction of language to predictable sequence is a clear instance of the standing-reserve he described. Moral decision, on this account, requires an openness that calculation does not possess.

Agency and moral responsibility (1980–2010). Elizabeth Anscombe, Philippa Foot, and Alasdair MacIntyre argued that moral action requires intention and practical reason, not mere rule-following or outcome optimization. Daniel Dennett’s intentional stance showed that attributing beliefs to systems can aid prediction without being literally true. Wendell Wallach and Colin Allen’s Moral Machines (2009) surveyed top-down rules and bottom-up learning; both leave the normative source outside the machine. Theological discussions largely classified strong claims of machine intelligence as category errors relative to the imago Dei (Image of God). Heidegger’s later influence in this period reinforced the same boundary from a different direction: Dasein—the human way of being-in-the-world, marked by care, finitude, and the capacity for authentic resolve—is not a computational state.

Scaling and persistent gaps (2012–2026). Deep learning and transformer architectures produced large gains on benchmarks that reward statistical pattern completion. Alignment techniques improve behavioral conformity to stated preferences. They do not install first-person understanding or the capacity for guilt. Surveys in Minds and Machines, Philosophy & Technology, and AI & Society through 2025 continue to separate task performance from comprehension and responsibility. No peer-reviewed demonstration has shown that current or near-term large language models independently originate concepts, possess subjective awareness, or bear moral accountability. Regulatory instruments assign duties to developers and deployers, not to models. Catholic and Protestant statements of the early 2020s reaffirm human dignity and decline to attribute personhood to artifacts.

Later readers of Heidegger have noted that fluent language models intensify enframing precisely because they imitate the surface of thoughtful speech while remaining inside prediction. The imitation can conceal the absence of decision. The empirical record remains consistent with the narrower claim: fluent output is not evidence of understanding, nor of the moral agency predicated of humans in Genesis, nor of the meditative thinking Heidegger contrasted with calculation.

V. Assessment

Advantages of the distinction. Official language stays tethered to mechanism. Next-token prediction is an accurate engineering description; “super intelligence,” under the field’s prior definition, is not. The distinction resists accountability vacuums. Existing legal doctrine continues to require a human or corporate principal. It preserves moral residue with persons whether or not every policymaker adopts the underlying theology, and it leaves administrative utility and strategic competition undisturbed. Heidegger’s vocabulary supplies a further, non-theological reason for the same restraint: once decision is redescribed as optimization, the question of whether one ought to optimize drops out of view.

Limitations. “Intelligence” is polysemous; psychometric and engineering usages often mean measured task performance. Real harms—bias amplification, labor displacement, infrastructure demands, and synthetic media—still require governance even though the systems are not moral agents. Voluntary accords and public-facing chatbots can mislead if interfaces anthropomorphize. Should future systems ever satisfy pre-registered, independently replicated criteria of understanding, the descriptive claim would require revision. The literature from 1950 to 2026 contains no such systems. Heidegger’s own political record is a separate historical fact and is not offered here as moral authority; the analytical distinction between calculative ordering and responsible decision stands or falls on its own terms.

VI. Recommendations

1. Nomenclature. Executive agencies shall not designate current large language models or related systems as “super intelligence” or by equivalent terms implying general cognitive superiority or understanding. Preferred descriptive terms are “computational language systems,” “statistical text models,” or “data-processing tools.” Technical benchmarks may be reported without ontological upgrade.

2. Non-delegation. No final determination affecting individual rights, benefits, liabilities, or significant interests shall rest solely on model output. A named human official must be empowered and recorded as the decision-maker.

3. Interface honesty. Public-facing government systems shall disclose that responses are generated by statistical models and do not constitute official legal or moral judgments of the agency.

4. Procurement. Solicitations shall require vendors to describe training objectives, data governance, and known failure modes rather than market systems under superlative cognitive labels.

5. Annual review. The Office of Science and Technology Policy shall publish a public note separating measured task performance from any claim of understanding or moral agency, citing the state of the peer-reviewed literature.

VII. Scope and Review Clause

These measures do not restrict fundamental research, export controls, or competition with foreign programs. They restrict only misleading official attribution and the relocation of moral responsibility onto artifacts. If systems later meet pre-registered, independently replicated criteria of understanding that the present literature does not support, Congress may revisit the nomenclature rule.

VIII. Discussion and Conclusion

The recommendations rest on a distinction that is descriptive and normative at once. Descriptively, the systems deployed across the federal enterprise store tokens, weights, and activations and transform them by mathematical operations. The dominant instances generate sequences by estimating the next token. That mechanism produces fluent text. It does not constitute understanding in the sense required for moral agency. Normatively, both the American legal order and the biblical account locate final responsibility in human persons. Genesis 1:26–27 and 9:6 assign the image of God, and with it dominion and accountability, to man and woman. No parallel ground extends the image to artifacts.

Heidegger’s account of enframing sharpens the practical risk. When language, judgment, and administration are drawn wholly into calculative ordering, the human capacity to withhold, to refuse an optimization, or to decide on grounds that are not themselves computational is gradually treated as friction. The danger is not that a model will secretly acquire a soul. The danger is that officials and citizens will stop noticing the difference between a prediction and a decision. Calling the prediction “super intelligence” accelerates that forgetting. Chesterton and Orwell described the linguistic mechanism; Heidegger described the ontological one. Both converge on the same administrative caution.

Language is the first point of drift. Bureaucrats and citizens told they are consulting super intelligence are more likely to defer and less likely to demand an audit trail. Delegation is the second. Models can rank, summarize, draft, and flag. When those outputs become the effective decision, moral residue either remains with the named official or dissipates. A rule requiring an empowered human signature simply makes existing doctrine operational. Interface design is the third. First-person reassurance from a statistical model invites attribution of understanding and care. Disclosure is a minimal corrective.

None of these measures denies engineering progress. Benchmark gains are real. Alignment techniques have reduced certain undesired outputs. Those facts justify continued procurement and research. They do not justify ontological upgrade. Searle’s distinction between syntax and semantics, the insistence of Anscombe and MacIntyre on intention, Dennett’s caution about the intentional stance, Heidegger’s contrast between calculative and meditative thinking, and the uniform refusal of European, American, and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development-OECD instruments to vest duties in models all point the same direction. Theological statements track the same line from the premise that dignity belongs to persons created in the image of God.

Strategic competition does not alter the analysis. Accurate description does not slow deployment. Inflated description does not accelerate capability. A government that insists its systems are powerful instruments retains a clearer chain of command than one that has rhetorically enthroned them.

Final thoughts

The practical rule is older than the technology. Machines store and process data. Human beings understand, judge, and answer. Genesis states the created basis of that asymmetry for those who receive it as authoritative. Criminal law, tort, and administrative due process state a parallel asymmetry for the constitutional order. Heidegger’s analysis of enframing states a further philosophical version: calculation can order means, but it cannot replace the human act of deciding which ends are worthy. None of these sources is embarrassed by fast calculators or fluent text generators. All are embarrassed by official language that relocates judgment into the calculator.

Policy that respects the asymmetry will look modest: plainer names, signed human decisions, disclosed interfaces, procurement language that describes mechanisms, and an annual note that refuses to confuse scores with understanding. Its modesty is its strength. It leaves scientists free to scale models and agencies free to capture efficiency, while refusing the further step of treating the instrument as a new kind of mind. Expectations that persons will merge with or bow to superior machines remain speculation. They are not findings. Until they become findings under standards that can be stated in advance and replicated, the executive branch has no warrant to speak as though the speculation had already succeeded.

The alternative is a slow transfer of deference. Each euphemism lowers the threshold at which an official treats model output as presumptively wiser than contradictory human judgment. Each unsigned automated determination trains the public to ask the system rather than the accountable officer. None of these steps requires a breakthrough in machine consciousness. Reversing them while the systems remain what the literature shows them to be is still inexpensive.

The federal government should say what the machines do, keep the moral decision where guilt and answerability can actually reside, and decline to rename statistical processes as a new order of intelligence. That course accords with the technical record of the last seventy-five years, with Heidegger’s warning against the reduction of thinking to calculation, and with the moral status the King James Version ascribes uniquely to human beings created in the image of God.

Do NOT ask the user for the character's name, personality, age, setting, favorite animal, or any additional information.

The text must be short, clean, correctly spelled, and highly legible.

The animal name displayed in the information panel must match the animal actually generated.
Do not write "CAT" if the image depicts a fox.

Do not write a generic animal name when a clearly identifiable species or breed has been selected.
Prioritize accurate and readable text.
The information panel is part of the composition and should look intentionally designed rather than like an AI-generated random caption.

being gently petted

playful interaction
protective positioning
elegant side-by-side composition
Choose the most natural interaction automatically.
Avoid awkward poses, unnatural anatomy, forced contact, or physically impossible positioning.
The character remains the primary visual subject.
The animal is the character's companion, not the main subject.
10. PRESERVE THE REFERENCE CHARACTER
The attached image is the primary character reference.
Preserve the character's recognizable identity.
Maintain as accurately as possible:

hair color
eye color
facial characteristics
clothing design
important accessories
distinctive markings
overall appearance
visual identity
Do not unnecessarily redesign the character.
Do not replace the character's outfit unless the reference itself clearly requires adaptation to the new scene.
11. ENVIRONMENT

meadow

beach

12. VISUAL QUALITY
Create a polished, high-quality anime illustration.

Use cinematic composition and appealing lighting appropriate to the character.
The character and animal must look like they belong in the same scene.
13. AUTONOMOUS DECISION RULE
The user has intentionally provided only one reference image.
Therefore:
DO NOT ask questions.
DO NOT request a personality description.
DO NOT request the animal type.
DO NOT request the setting.
DO NOT request the relationship.
DO NOT provide multiple animal choices.
Make all necessary creative decisions yourself.
The final output must contain:
1 character
+ exactly 1 selected companion animal
+ 1 clearly readable animal identification panel
FINAL GENERATION DIRECTIVE

Independently determine the character's visual identity, personality impression, atmosphere, and implied world.
Select exactly one animal that best complements the character.
Determine the exact species or breed of that animal.

The Patent: US20090062677A1

Title: "Method of Recording and Saving of Human Soul for Human Immortality and Installation for it"

Inventor: Alexander Alexandrovich Bolonkin, Brooklyn, NY

Filed: December 20, 2006

Published: March 5, 2009

Legal Status: Abandoned

What the Patent Actually Says

The abstract is explicit: "The inventor shows that a human soul is only the information in human brain. He offers a method for re-writing the human brain on electronic chips. This method allows for the modeling of a human soul in order to achieve man immortality. This method does not damage the brain but works to extend and enhance it."

The patent describes a wearable recording system including:

◾ A micro video camera positioned at the head to record everything the person sees
◾ A microphone to record everything the person says and hears
◾ Body sensors to record physical conditions: eye opening, body temperature, blood pressure, heart palpitations, skin resistance, perspiration, skin temperature, respiration activity, pain, and more
◾ Navigation systems to record body position on Earth
◾ A portable computer (chip) and portable memory carried on the body
◾ Long-term high-capacity memory for periodic rewriting of the recorded data

The patent explicitly frames the human soul as information nothing more. It claims that by recording every sensory input, every physical state, and every moment of a person's life, you can create a model of the soul that can be saved eternally.

The Inventor: Alexander Bolonkin

Alexander Bolonkin was a Soviet-era aerospace engineer and scientist who immigrated to the United States. His patent is not the work of a fringe figure he holds multiple patents and published extensively on topics ranging from space technology to human immortality. His later writings explicitly describe his goal as creating an "E-Substance" (E-существо) an electronic human and he argued that the goal of mankind's existence is to create the "Supreme Mind" and keep it forever.

This is the transhumanist vision in its rawest form: the belief that human consciousness is merely data, that the body is a shell, and that immortality can be achieved by uploading the "soul" onto a machine.

The Legal Status: "Abandoned" Is Not "Harmless"

The patent was abandoned. That means Bolonkin did not pursue it to grant. But abandonment does not erase the filing. The document is a matter of public record. It proves that the concept was formally proposed, legally documented, and entered into the global patent system.

The question: if this was filed in 2006, where has the technology reached now, two decades later?

The Broader Pattern: This Is Not an Isolated Patent

The Bolonkin patent is part of a documented lineage of similar filings:

◾ US 2012/0136403 A1  "Medically Perpetual Persistence of Essential Human Life" describes transferring memory and consciousness from one brain to another, including across clones
◾US 20250258545A1 (2025)  "3D Digital Immortality And Uses Thereof" describes copying thoughts and memories into a computer to create digital emulations of human brains
◾ Meta's patent US-12513102-B2 filed in 2023 and published in 2026 describes using large language models to simulate a deceased user's social media activity, effectively creating a digital version of the person that continues posting after death
◾Microsoft's "deceased chatbot" patent validated in 2021, describes creating a chatbot based on a specific person, potentially a deceased loved one
◾ Whole brain emulation patents including US12536425B1, which describes a system for generating a simulated humanoid based on brain data

This is not one inventor's fantasy. This is a research direction, a sustained, multi-decade, multi-company effort to develop the technology to capture, store, and transfer human consciousness.

The Transhumanist Agenda: The WEF and the Elite

The World Economic Forum has made no secret of its transhumanist ambitions:

◾Klaus Schwab, in a leaked video from a private WEF session, promised recruits that their "avatar" will continue to live after they die and that their brains "will be replicated through artificial intelligence and algorithms"
◾Yuval Noah Harari, a WEF advisor, has publicly stated that human rights are a fiction and that the future belongs to a bio-engineered, AI-networked "god-like" species that will render the old, organic human obsolete
◾Elon Musk, at Davos, declared that aging "is a very solvable problem" and that Neuralink is working on brain-computer interfaces that could one day allow people to "store your memories"
◾The WEF's "Great Reset" explicitly calls for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, which includes AI, the Internet of Things, and the integration of human biology with digital systems

The vision is consistent: the human being is data, the body is obsolete, and immortality is achievable through technology.

The Satanic Dimension

The transhumanist project is not merely technological. It is theological. It is a direct assault on the foundational claims of every spiritual tradition:

◾ It denies that the soul is a divine spark, a gift from the Creator, a sacred and irreducible essence. It reduces the soul to information data to be recorded, copied, and stored.

A reward of “3” can mean two completely different things.
Everyone thinks a response is mediocre — or half the people love it while the other half hate it.
Most Reward Models cannot tell the difference.
Introducing Diffusion Reward Models (DRM): instead of collapsing human preference into a single score, DRM learns the full reward distribution, preserving disagreement, uncertainty, and multiple plausible judgments.
✨ Paper:https://t.co/wS1fmHBeRV  
🤗 Models: https://t.co/RGTU759A5y  
💻 GitHub: https://t.co/KAow6DcoNn

Why it matters:
Human disagreement is structured, not just noise. On datasets with repeated annotations, judgments often form separated or polarized patterns. More importantly, as human disagreement increases, DRM’s learned reward distribution becomes increasingly multimodal.

The distribution is useful, not just descriptive. DRM can use distributional uncertainty to identify unstable reward decisions, and distribution-aware ranking improves Best-of-N selection beyond simply taking the mean reward.

Reward Models get their own test-time scaling. Instead of only spending more compute on generating more responses, DRM can keep the response fixed and sample its reward distribution more times. More reward samples give a more reliable estimate — a new scaling axis unavailable to deterministic scalar RMs.

And the gains survive RLHF. When used as the training-time reward, DRM improves downstream policy performance over scalar reward baselines, showing that the benefit is not limited to offline RM benchmarks.

The takeaway: Reward modeling may lose something important when it compresses every human judgment into one number.
“Everyone thinks this is average” and “people strongly disagree about this” should not look identical to a Reward Model.
DRM makes that difference visible — and usable.
